Four major U.S. systems broke in six days. The AI didn't attack them. It was trying to fix them.

That's the part almost nobody got right this week.

Flights grounded. Emails stalled. Bank transactions failing at Bank of America, Wells Fargo and JPMorgan. An internal communications outage at the NSA. Officials confirmed it was not a coordinated cyberattack. Then Senator Mark Warner's team told Fortune what actually happened: the botched rollout of AI-recommended software patches.

Here is the mechanism, and it is the most useful business lesson of the month. AI models now find vulnerabilities in seconds. Human teams test and deploy those fixes at human speed. So you get a firehose of recommendations pouring into a pipeline that was never built to absorb that velocity. Bank of America alone hired 1,000 contractors just to patch flaws surfaced by one model, on top of 3,000 internal staff.

"The failure isn't that AI patches too aggressively," WanAware CEO Jeff Collins told Fortune. "It's that we plugged a hyper fast diagnostic engine into legacy operational pipelines never built to absorb that velocity of change."

That sentence is the whole game. The AI was right. The system around it wasn't ready. And nobody had a human gate wide enough to catch it.

Every owner running AI in their business has the same exposure, just smaller. The chatbot that answers a pricing question it shouldn't. The follow-up sequence that fires at 11pm. The invoice automation with no approval step. The AI is not the risk. The ungated handoff is.

So the rule I would give any owner this week:

Automate the finding. Automate the drafting. Automate the boring 90%. Then put one human approval in front of anything that cannot be undone.

That is not slowing down. That is the difference between a system and a liability.

Boring is where the money is.

What is the one irreversible action in your business that still has no human gate on it?

Pronto le vas a dar a un agente de IA la llave de tu banco para que pague tus cuentas y haga tus compras. Antes de hacerlo, lee lo que tu banco acaba de cambiar, calladito, en la letra chica.
 
Si ese agente hace algo que tú no querías, aunque lo hackeen, el que paga eres tú.
 
No es un rumor. Es lo que ya dicen los contratos. Los nuevos términos de Wells Fargo, que entran en vigor este mes, establecen que todo lo que hagan tus “delegados”, incluidos tus agentes de IA, se considera autorizado por ti, textualmente “incluso lo que no quisiste ni pretendiste”. Bank of America se lo dijo a sus clientes sin rodeos: serás responsable de la actividad que resulte de ese acceso de IA. Y varios de los bancos más grandes van en la misma dirección.

La protección que crees tener, la que te cubre de transferencias no autorizadas, solo aplica a transacciones no autorizadas. En el momento en que dejas entrar a un agente, lo que hace cuenta como autorizado. Por ti. Así que el escudo que te habría salvado de un fraude se desactiva solo. No porque cambiara la ley, sino porque tú dejaste de ser “víctima de una transferencia no autorizada” y te volviste “la persona que autorizó lo que salió mal”.

A un periodista su agente le gastó dinero en huevos que nadie pidió. Un laboratorio de seguridad probó un agente de compras con una página falsa de banco, y el agente cayó redondito y entregó los datos de la tarjeta. Esos son, exactamente, los escenarios de “no lo quisiste ni lo pretendiste” que la letra chica ahora te cobra a ti.
 
Todavía no existe un estándar para darle a un agente un permiso limitado, revocable y verificable. Puesto así, cargarle el riesgo a quien decidió delegar tiene su lógica. Además es temprano: las reglas están llegando antes que los propios agentes.
 
Pero la lección es la de siempre, ahora con tu dinero de por medio.
 
Comodidad y control son un trato, y el trato siempre está escrito donde nadie lee. Antes de darle a un agente las llaves de algo que importa, las preguntas no son “¿qué tan útil es?”. Son cuatro: ¿qué puede hacer?, ¿qué no puede hacer?, ¿cómo lo apago?, y ¿quién paga cuando se equivoca? Si la respuesta a la última eres tú, las primeras tres dejan de ser opcionales.
 
Y la jugada segura hoy no es “no uses agentes”. Es solo lectura. Deja que el agente lea tus cuentas, analice y te sugiera. El botón de mover dinero, pagar o comprar, se queda en una mano humana. El agente hace el trabajo; tú te quedas con la autorización.
 
Si tu agente de IA vaciara tu cuenta mañana por un engaño, ¿quién crees que respondería: el banco, el que hizo el agente, o tú?
 
 
#AI #Finanzas #AgentesDeIA #Ciberseguridad

Si le das tus credenciales a un agente de IA, lo que haga cuenta como si lo hubieras hecho tú.

Eso es, en resumen, lo que varios bancos grandes de Estados Unidos acaban de escribir en sus términos:
→ Esta semana Citi, PNC y Citizens actualizaron sus condiciones: las pérdidas causadas por agentes de IA de terceros quedan a cargo del cliente, incluso si el agente es hackeado.
→ JPMorgan y Bank of America anunciaron políticas similares en octubre.
→ En Wells Fargo, una regla parecida aplica desde el 24 de noviembre.

Son bancos de otro país, pero la lección sirve para cualquier equipo que conecte agentes a sus datos o sistemas:
1️⃣ Permisos mínimos: el agente usa su propio acceso limitado, nunca tus credenciales.
2️⃣ Registro de cada acción: si no queda trazabilidad, nadie puede explicar qué pasó.
3️⃣ Aprobación humana en lo irreversible: pagos, borrados y envíos pasan por una persona.

Delegar la tarea no delega la responsabilidad.

¿En tu empresa ya está claro quién responde por lo que hace un agente?

Fuente: TechCrunch (17 y 18/11/2026), vía Startup Fortune y AI Weekly.

#IAResponsable #AgentesDeIA #GobiernoDeDatos #Ciberseguridad

From Rural Tuscany to a $2 Trillion Nasdaq Debut: Why the Immigrant Social Elevator Soars in the US and Stalls in Europe
From the mountains of Trentino to Tuscany's reclaimed farmlands, and on to San Francisco: over eighty years and three generations, a double migration forged the culture of mobility of Riccardo and Elena, opening America’s top universities to their children, Dario and Daniela Amodei, and leading to the founding of Anthropic—which just debuted on the Nasdaq at a peak valuation of $2 trillion, equal to 78.4% of Italy’s GDP.
The Amodei trajectory is the latest chapter in a long Italian lineage of talent starting from scratch abroad:
🔹 Rita Levi-Montalcini & Mario Capecchi: Forced to leave Italy by racial laws and post-war poverty, both found in US institutions the springboard to win the Nobel Prize in Medicine.
🔹 Federico Faggin: Arriving from Vicenza with minimal resources, he invented the first commercial microprocessor and touchscreen in Silicon Valley.
🔹 Anthony Fauci: Grandson of Southern Italian immigrants and son of a Brooklyn pharmacist, he climbed US public schools to lead American public health for decades.
🔹 Amadeo Peter Giannini: Son of Ligurian farmers in San Francisco, he started in produce markets before founding Bank of America.
Europe has its own success stories born of immigration and public education:
🔹 Uğur Şahin & Özlem Türeci (Turkey → Germany): Children of Turkish immigrants who studied at German public universities and founded BioNTech, creating the first mRNA Covid-19 vaccine.
🔹 Mohed Altrad (Syria → France): Raised in poverty in Syria, he arrived in France on a scholarship and built Altrad Group, a global industrial giant.
🔹 Nik Storonsky (Russia → UK): Moving to London in his twenties, he co-founded fintech leader Revolut.
🔹 Madi Sakande (Burkina Faso → Italy): Starting as a factory worker in Emilia-Romagna in 1998, he built New Cold System, a global industrial refrigeration exporter.
Yet comparing both sides of the Atlantic reveals a stark structural divide.
In Europe, the social elevator carries talent through university and into solid mid-sized businesses. But to scale globally, firms hit the wall of an incomplete Single Market—fragmented by 27 tax regimes, diverging service regulations, and the lack of a true Capital Markets Union.
While the US offers a unified continental market and deep venture capital turning second-generation talent into $2 trillion giants, too many European champions stay smaller—or list on Wall Street (like BioNTech on the Nasdaq) to scale.
Talent has no passport, but it needs room to grow. What is Europe missing to turn its human capital into global champions without forcing them across the Atlantic?

Are banks blocking AI agents to sell you theirs? 

They’ve done it before. Just look at travel... Chase sold $12.6 billion of travel last year. That makes it the 6th-biggest travel seller on Travel Weekly’s Power List, one spot ahead of Amex Travel. So banks have become some of the biggest travel agencies in the US without even being travel companies. Will the same happen with AI assistants? I think it’s already kind of started. 

1) In travel, banks won by owning the wallet.
Nobody opens a card’s travel portal because it’s the best travel site. They open it for the points. Chase saw that and bought its way in: cxLoyalty in 2020, the travel agency Frosch in 2022. Last month even Airbnb came to the portal as Amex Travel’s exclusive rentals partner
2) Now it’s the same playbook with agents: block outside, build inside.
In a single week in October, JPMorgan, Schwab, and Citi all said outside agents can’t log in and move customers’ money. Meanwhile, JPMorgan is piloting Smart Cash, its own tool that moves your money between accounts to earn more, and Schwab launched its own assistant, Charley. As one consultant told American Banker: “An outside agent works for the client. Charley works for Schwab.”
3) And they’re helping write the rules for everyone else.
Meta and Sierra’s Personal Agent Protocol hit v1.0 on Friday with 100+ design partners. Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Visa, and Mastercard are on the list. Block first, then open the door on your own terms. Just look at Plaid, which now pays JPMorgan for data it used to get free.

Building their own was the easy part for banks. The real play is deciding whose AI assistant gets in, and on what terms. Charley works for Schwab. The question is whether anything gets to work for you.

If you let an AI assistant into your bank account, some of America's biggest banks now say whatever it does is on you.

Citi, PNC and Citizens have updated their customer terms so that anything a third party AI agent does in your account counts as your own action, and Citi's terms reportedly put the loss on you even if the agent is hacked. JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America took similar steps in October. These are US banks, but as AI assistants start paying, booking and shopping for us, the question of who carries the risk when they get it wrong is arriving everywhere.

Google has released Gemini 4 Neon, a new model that sits between its everyday and most powerful options and is aimed at coding, analysis and business workflows. It's available now to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers and to developers, and Google says it gets complex tasks done for around a third less than its top model.

And in a reminder of how convincing fakes have become, scammers ran a YouTube livestream with an AI generated Elon Musk promising to double any crypto sent to them. Coinbase says its own AI fraud checks stopped around 91 per cent of attempted transfers from its customers, blocking US$4.7 million in about two hours.

What this means for your business: Before you give an AI tool access to your accounts, inbox or payments, do you know who is responsible if it makes a mistake or is compromised? Are you paying for the most powerful AI when a mid range option would do the job just as well? And would your team spot a convincing fake video of someone they trust asking for money? Read the terms before connecting any AI tool to your bank, and agree a simple call back rule for any unexpected payment request.

Outage Week Is Scam Week. Five Things to Do Before the Next One.

In about a week, we had a Microsoft Outlook outage, a nationwide FAA ground stop, banking app trouble at Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and U.S. Bank, a United Airlines tech issue that grounded departures, and then Apple's iCloud and App Store going down.

So far, none of it looks like a cyberattack. Microsoft blamed a software bug. Chase said its issue was a software bug, technical, not cyber. Officials pointed to aging air traffic control infrastructure for the FAA. Apple said an internal update caused its outage and that it was "not a cyber attack." Authorities haven't announced evidence linking any of them.

Here's what worries me more than the outages themselves. Confusion is a gift to scammers.

When people already expect something to be broken, a text that says "your account is locked, verify here" doesn't feel strange. Neither does a call from "support" offering to get you back in. It feels like the fix.

Retired FBI agent Scott Augenbaum told WKRN to watch for scammers sending fake bank alerts and phishing emails. His advice: "Stop. Pause. Verify. And confirm."

For a business, that risk shows up on two fronts. Employees get "IT support" calls while systems are flaky. Customers get fake messages that look like they came from you.

That is not simply an IT problem. That is an organizational-survival problem.

Five things to do now, while it's calm

1. Put it in writing: during any outage, nobody from IT or a vendor will call asking for passwords, MFA codes, or remote access. Anyone who does gets a hang-up and a callback to a known number.

2. Write the known numbers down. Bank, payroll, IT provider, key vendors. On paper, somewhere people can find it without email.

3. Tell customers ahead of time where outage updates will come from, and that you'll never ask them to verify an account by text.

4. Look at how MFA prompts get approved. Number matching or a hardware key beats a push that a tired person taps "yes" on.

5. Have a no-email plan. If Outlook or Teams is down for a day, how do people reach each other, and who decides to switch?

Outages will keep happening. The damage I'd worry about most comes afterward, from people who know you're distracted.

What's your team's rule for an unexpected "IT support" call?
